context: He has just carried Dante across the river of boiling blood on his back (Canto 12) and is wading back to the far bank.

quote: a wood unmarked by any path
note: The second dark wood of the poem, after the forest of Canto 1. That one could be escaped. This one is made of the souls of people who killed themselves.

quote: not green but dark and withered
note: Three lines in a row built on "not this, but that". The canto is full of such balanced, artificial turns of phrase, in the manner of the court rhetoric its main speaker was famous for.
A river and a town that marked the limits of the Maremma, the wild, marshy coast of Tuscany, thick with scrub and known for its boar. Corneto is now called Tarquinia.

context: In Aeneid 3 they swoop on the Trojans' meal on the Strophades islands and foul it, and one of them, Celaeno, foretells that hunger will one day make the Trojans eat their own tables.

note: The seventh circle, for the violent, has three rings, one inside the other. The first was the river of blood, for those violent against others. This wood holds those violent against themselves. The burning sand ahead is for the violent against God, nature and art.

quote: I think he thought I might be thinking
note: A famous tongue-twister in the Italian: "Cred'io ch'ei credette ch'io credesse". The knotted wording suits the tangled wood, and prepares for the ornate speech of the courtier who is about to talk.
The souls of suicides are shut inside these trees. They can speak only when a branch is broken, so every word comes out with blood and pain.

quote: We were men once, now we are trees
note: The punishment fits the act. They rejected their human bodies, so they are denied human form and given a lower kind of life, that of plants, which medieval thought ranked below animals.

quote: Like a green log burning at one end
note: A simile from the hearth: damp wood on a fire hisses and oozes sap from the end that isn't burning. Here the hiss is speech and the sap is blood.

quote: what he had seen only in my verses
note: In Aeneid 3, Aeneas pulls up a shrub in Thrace and it bleeds and speaks: it has grown from the grave of the murdered Trojan prince Polydorus. Virgil says Dante had to see the thing for himself to believe it.
Fame among the living is the one thing the damned can still hope to gain, and Virgil offers it again and again in Hell to get souls to talk.

quote: the one who held both keys
context: He never gives his name, only his office. The two keys are yes and no: he decided what the emperor granted and what he refused.
Pier served him for nearly thirty years and still calls him worthy of honor. Dante has already placed Frederick himself in Hell, among the heretics (Inferno 10).

note: Envy, pictured as a prostitute who never takes her eyes off the court. Pier says the envy of other courtiers destroyed him.
The emperor's court. Caesar and Augustus, three lines on, are titles of the Holy Roman Emperor, who claimed to be the heir of the Roman emperors. Both mean Frederick.
Dante gives Pier the elaborate style of his own Latin letters, full of wordplay and paired opposites: locking and unlocking, honors and grief, just and unjust.

The heart of his story. He claims he was innocent of treason, and Dante seems to believe him. But by killing himself to escape disgrace he did an injustice to an innocent man: himself. That, not treason, is why he is here.

quote: By the strange roots of this wood
note: A man swears by what is most his own. All Pier has left is the tree he has become.
Dante is too moved to speak. Like Pier, he was a poet and a public servant, and he too would be brought down by false charges: Florence exiled him in 1302.
The soul threw its body away without care, so it gets no chosen place here. It lands by chance and takes root where it falls.
Dante's word is spelt, a coarse grain that sprouts in many shoots.

quote: create pain and a vent for pain
note: The Harpies tear the leaves, which hurts, and the wounds they make are the only openings through which the souls can cry out.
Christian teaching holds that at the Last Judgment every soul is reunited with its body. Dante makes a grim exception of his own for the suicides: they will fetch their bodies but never wear them.
Each body will hang forever from the tree that holds its soul, in plain sight and out of reach: a wood of hanged corpses.

A different group in the same ring: men who destroyed their own wealth with such violence that it amounted to self-destruction. They are not the spendthrifts of Canto 7, who merely spent too freely. Here they are hunted through the wood like game.
He calls for a second death that would end him for good. It cannot come.

A young man of Siena, said to have belonged to the Spendthrift Brigade, a club of rich Sienese who ran through their fortunes (Inferno 29). Early commentators say that, ruined, he chose to die in battle rather than live poor.
A bitter joke. It was no tournament but a rout: in 1288 the men of Arezzo ambushed a Sienese force at Pieve al Toppo. Lano was killed there. The taunt is that he ran faster now than he did then.
Dante's Italian makes them bitches. They tear the squanderers apart as these men tore apart their own estates. Some readers see in them the creditors, or the poverty, that hounded them in life.

A nobleman of Padua, notorious for wasting a great inheritance. Early commentators tell of him setting fire to his own houses to enjoy the blaze. He is said to have been killed in 1239 on the orders of the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano.

context: The bush names its city by a legend. Pagan Florence had Mars, god of war, as its patron, and on becoming Christian replaced him with John the Baptist.

note: The art of Mars is war. Slighted by the change of patron, the god punishes Florence with endless fighting among its own citizens. The speaker is a Christian soul talking like a superstitious pagan.

quote: at the crossing of the Arno
note: A worn fragment of an ancient statue, believed to be Mars, stood at the head of the Ponte Vecchio in Dante's day. Florentines thought the city's safety depended on it. A flood carried it away in 1333.

A confusion Dante shared with the chroniclers of his time. Attila the Hun never reached Florence. The legend of the city's destruction belongs to Totila, king of the Ostrogoths, who besieged it in the sixth century, and even he did not level it.

quote: I made a gallows of my own house
note: He hanged himself at home. Dante leaves him nameless. Early commentators proposed two Florentines, the judge Lotto degli Agli and the bankrupt Rocco de' Mozzi, and some thought he stands for Florence itself, a city destroying itself from within.
